# Types and numbers

@difference Extension: the integers `Byte`, `UByte`, `Short`, `UShort`, `UInt`, `Long`, `ULong` and the reals `Half` and `Double` work everywhere a type can be written; number literals take suffixes (`255ui8`, `0.1.d`); conversions, saturating versions, bit functions and Double math; `Void` as a return type.

The originals have three kinds of values: the integer `Int` (32 bits), the real `Float` (32 bits) and `String`, plus the custom types you declare with `Type`. A program that uses none of the types below behaves exactly as before.

## The types

| Type | Short form | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `Byte`, `UByte` | | 8 bits, with and without a sign |
| `Short`, `UShort` | | 16 bits, with and without a sign |
| `Int` | `%` | 32 bits, with a sign |
| `UInt` | | 32 bits, without a sign |
| `Long`, `ULong` | `%%` (`Long`) | 64 bits, with and without a sign |
| `Half` | | 16-bit real |
| `Float` | `#` | 32-bit real |
| `Double` | `##` | 64-bit real |
| `String` | `$` | text |
| custom type | `.Name` | a `Type` you declared |

Every one of them works as a `Global`, a `Local`, a parameter (with default values), a return type, a field of a `Type`, a `Const` and the type of a `Dim` array. Write the type in the short form with a sign after the name (`Count%`, `Total#`) or in the long form with `:Type` (`Count:UInt`, `Function Now:ULong()`). A function with the name of a type converts to it (`Byte(x)`, `UInt(x)`, `Double(x)`, next to the `Int`, `Float` and `Str` of the originals). The tables of built-in functions in the compiler can use the same types for parameters and return values (`b B h H i I l u x f d s`), not just `i f s`. `tests/suite/language_types.bb` checks the combinations.

## Calculations and conversions

The originals have two kinds of numbers: a 32-bit integer (`Int`) and a 32-bit real (`Float`). BlitzLLVM also has the integers `Byte`, `UByte`, `Short`, `UShort`, `UInt`, `Long` and `ULong` (8, 16, 32 and 64 bits, with and without a sign), and the reals `Half` and `Double`. A variable gets one of these types with `name:Type`, and a function of the same name as the type converts to it (`Byte(x)`, `UInt(x)`, `Double(x)` and so on, next to the `Int`, `Float` and `Str` that the originals have). A program that never uses them behaves exactly as before.

* Calculations promote to at least 32 bits: a `Byte` plus a `Byte` is an `Int`, and the result only goes back to 8 bits when it is assigned to a `Byte` again. Unsigned wins when the widths are equal, so a `UInt` and an `Int` make a `UInt`, and a `Long` and a `ULong` make a `ULong`. Reals promote to at least a `Float`.
* Converting a whole number to a smaller type keeps its lowest bits (`Byte(200)` is -56, `UByte(-1)` is 255), and to a larger type keeps its value, extending the sign of a signed type and filling with 0 for an unsigned one. The `Sat` versions ([SatByte](SatByte), [SatUByte](SatUByte), [SatShort](SatShort), [SatUShort](SatUShort), [SatInt](SatInt), [SatUInt](SatUInt), [SatLong](SatLong), [SatULong](SatULong)) stop at the smallest and largest number of the type instead.
* Converting a real to a whole number rounds to the nearest whole number (halves go to the even one, as `Int` does in the original) and stops at the smallest and largest number of the type, with a real that is not a number becoming 0. `Int(10000000000.0)` is 2147483647.
* [Abs](Language) and `Sgn` see an unsigned number as never negative, and `Min`, `Max`, comparisons, division and `Mod` of an unsigned number are done without a sign, and `Shr` fills with 0 for every type.
* [Sqr](Sqr), [Sin](Sin), [Cos](Cos), [Tan](Tan), [ASin](ASin), [ACos](ACos), [ATan](ATan), [ATan2](ATan2), [Floor](Floor), [Ceil](Ceil), [Exp](Exp), [Log](Log) and [Log10](Log10) give a `Float` as in the original, unless an argument is a `Double`: then they calculate with a `Double` and give one. A `Long` or `ULong` argument is converted to a `Float` first, so convert it with `Double` to keep its digits. `^` already calculated with doubles.
* [PopCount](PopCount), [LeadingZeros](LeadingZeros), [TrailingZeros](TrailingZeros), [RotL](RotL), [RotR](RotR) and [ByteSwap](ByteSwap) work on the bits of a number with the width of its type.

## Number suffixes

A plain number is an `Int` (`5`) or a `Float` (`5.0`), as in the originals. BlitzLLVM can pick the type of a number by writing a suffix directly behind it, with no space. The suffix is not case sensitive.

| Suffix | Type | Suffix | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| `i8` | `Byte` | `.h`, `.fp16` | `Half` |
| `ui8` | `UByte` | `.f`, `.fp32` | `Float` |
| `i16` | `Short` | `.d`, `.fp64` | `Double` |
| `ui16` | `UShort` | `u` | `UInt`, or `ULong` if it needs more than 32 bits |
| `i32` | `Int` | | |
| `ui32` | `UInt` | | |
| `i64` | `Long` | | |
| `ui64` | `ULong` | | |

```blitzbasic
;run
Local big:Long = 5000000000i64
Local mask:UByte = 255ui8
Local tiny:Byte = -128i8
Local half:Half = 0.5h
Local exact:Double = 0.1.d
Print big
Print mask
Print tiny
Print half
Print exact
```

### Rules

* The whole number suffixes (`i8` to `ui64`, `u`) go on whole numbers: decimal, `0x` and `0b`. The real suffixes (`.h`, `.f`, `.d`, `.fp16`, `.fp32`, `.fp64`) go on every number when they start with a dot: `3.d`, `2.5.h`, `0b101.f` (5.0) and `0xFF.f` (255.0). The dot is what keeps them apart from the digits of a `0x` number: `0xFFf` is just the number 4095. A number that already has a decimal point may leave the dot out: `2.5h`, `0.1d` and `1.5fp16` are the same as `2.5.h`, `0.1.d` and `1.5.fp16`, while `5h` is an error. `$FF` and `%101` take no suffix.
* The suffix has to end the number: `1foo` is still the number 1 followed by a name, as before.
* A whole number without a suffix should fit into an `Int`. If it does not (`5000000000`), it is clamped to the largest `Int` like in the original, and the compiler warns about it ([literal-out-of-range](Warnings)), so a program that expects the real number is not surprised. Write `i64` or `ui64` (or `ui32`) behind it to keep the number. A `0x` or `0b` number of up to 32 bits is an `Int` with the same bits as `$FFFFFFFF`, so `0xFFFFFFFF` is -1.
* A number with a suffix has to fit into its type, or it is an error: `300i8` and `70000.h` do not compile. A `0x` or `0b` number is a bit pattern of the type and may use all of its bits, so `0xFFi8` is -1, `0xFFui8` is 255, and `0b11111111i8` is -1.
* A minus in front of a decimal number with a suffix belongs to the number, so `-128i8` is fine. Unsigned types can not be negative.
* The existing `u` suffix is unchanged: `5u` is a `UInt` and `5000000000u` a `ULong`.
* `-2147483648` without a suffix is -2147483647 (with the same warning), as in the original, which clamps 2147483648 to the largest `Int` before it negates it. Write `-2147483647 - 1` or `-2147483648i32` for the smallest `Int`.

## Void

`Function Name:Void(...)` declares a function that returns no data.

`Void` is only a return type, written in the long form (`Function Log:Void(message:String)`), and there is no short form. A `Void` function is called as a statement; `Return` inside of it takes no value, and giving it one is an error. Using a call of it as a value (`x = Log("a")`, `Print Log("a")`, `Return Log("a")`) or in a condition (`If`, `While`, `Until`, `Select`) is an error, too, because there is nothing to use. `Void` can not be the type of a parameter, a variable or a field. Without `Void`, a function that has no `Return value` still returns an `Int`, as in the originals.
